note: Every NASA number ASTRA shows comes from a fixture file listed here. The engine never makes a network call: the scripts in scripts/fetch/ download these files on a developer machine and the results are committed here. See docs/nasa-data-decisions.md for how each entry was obtained and what still needs checking.

sources.title: Earth-Mars observer range and one-way light time
sources.note: JPL Horizons observer table for Mars (COMMAND '499') seen from the Earth geocentre (CENTER '500@399'), daily steps from 2026-11-12 to 2028-05-05, quantities 20 (range, AU), 21 (one-way light time, min) and 23 (Sun-Observer-Target elongation, deg). Exact request URL: https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/api/horizons.api?format=text&COMMAND=%27499%27&CENTER=%27500%40399%27&EPHEM_TYPE=%27OBSERVER%27&START_TIME=%272026-11-12%27&STOP_TIME=%272028-05-05%27&STEP_SIZE=%271d%27&QUANTITIES=%2720%2C21%2C23%27&CSV_FORMAT=%27NO%27&EXTRA_PREC=%27YES%27. 541 rows (covers the spring-2028 solar conjunction); light time runs from 338.3 s to 1203.4 s over the window.

sources.title: ISS cabin air quality and crew radiation dose (Rodent Research 7)
sources.note: EDA mission RR-7 (2018-06-29 to 2018-09-18), the longest continuous cabin series in the EDA. Endpoints: /eda/api/missions/RR-7/co2/, /temperature/, /humidity/, /radiation_data/. UNIT CONVERSION: the EDA publishes CO2 in ppm and does not publish the cabin pressure, so we convert with the standard atmospheric pressure of 760 mmHg (mmHg = ppm / 1e6 * 760). TODO(verify): the ISS cabin actually runs near 14.5 psia (~735 mmHg), which would make the converted values about 3% lower; the EDA does not publish the cabin pressure, so 760 mmHg is used and recorded here. DATA CLEANING: 1534 of 21948 CO2 readings above 2x the series median were dropped as sensor spikes (the raw series contains readings up to 9000 ppm); the series was then averaged down to one reading per hour (1720 rows) to stay inside the 500 KB fixture budget. The first 124 hourly rows (to 2018-07-06) are a constant 200 ppm sensor fill, far below outdoor air (about 420 ppm); the engine and the simulator skip them.

sources.title: Inspiration4 astronaut blood and urine measurements
sources.note: WHICH STUDY HOLDS WHAT: OSD-575 holds the comprehensive metabolic panel (Quest Diagnostics CMP TRANSFORMED CSV: glucose, creatinine, sodium, potassium, ALT, calcium); OSD-569 holds the complete blood count (CBC TRANSFORMED CSV: white blood cells, haemoglobin, platelets, neutrophils, lymphocytes, hematocrit). Both were downloadable from https://osdr.nasa.gov/geode-py/ws/studies/{study}/download?source=datamanager&file={file}. 336 values from four real crew members (C001-C004) across seven timepoints (L-92, L-44, L-3, R+1, R+45, R+82, R+194 days relative to launch). Reference ranges are the dataset's own Quest Diagnostics ranges, carried through unchanged. Note: the CBC CSV reports haemoglobin as a percentage in this dataset, so the grams-per-decilitre columns are used instead.

sources.title: DONKI solar particle events (September-October 2021)
sources.note: Fetched from CCMC's DONKI API (https://ccmc.gsfc.nasa.gov/DONKI-API/get/SEP and /FLR), no key needed, for 2021-10-01 to 2021-11-30: 11 solar particle events and 23 flares. The old kauai.ccmc.gsfc.nasa.gov/DONKI/WS/ hosts time out from our network and api.nasa.gov's shared DEMO_KEY is rate-limited (HTTP 429). CCMC answers HTTP 403 to a User-Agent containing an e-mail address, so the fetch scripts send a plain one. ASTRA replays sepID 2021-10-28T16:35:00-SEP-001, GOES-P's >100 MeV detection of the 28 Oct 2021 event (the first ground-level enhancement of solar cycle 25). The event time, instrument and link are real; the replay dose (10 mSv over 24 h unsheltered), the 10-minute shelter delay and the 0.25 shelter factor in donki/replay.json are illustrative ASTRA numbers, not DONKI measurements.

sources.title: NASA-STD-3001 Volume 1: Crew Health (Rev C)
sources.note: The career dose limit comes from requirement [V1 4030] in section 4.8.2 (page 39): 'An individual crewmember's total career effective radiation dose due to spaceflight radiation exposure shall be less than 600 mSv.' That is the 600 mSv limit ASTRA shows. PDF: https://www.nasa.gov/reference/nasa-std-3001/nasa-std-3001-vol-1-rev-c-with-signature.pdf

sources.title: NASA-STD-3001 Volume 2: Human Factors, Habitability and Environmental Controls
sources.note: The one-hour CO2 limit comes from requirement [V2 6004] in section 6.2.1.3 (page 53): 'The system shall limit the average one-hour CO2 partial pressure (ppCO2) in the habitable volume to no more than 3 mmHg.' That is the 3.0 mmHg Act threshold ASTRA shows for cabin CO2. PDF: https://www.nasa.gov/reference/nasa-std-3001/nasa-std-3001-vol-2.pdf

sources.agency: NASA Office of Chief Health and Medical Officers
sources.title: Technical Brief: Carbon Dioxide (OCHMO-TB-004)
sources.note: The 7-day CO2 threshold comes from page 5 of the technical brief: 'To keep the risk of headache below 1%, average 7-day CO2 needs to be maintained below 2.5 mmHg (current ISS range: 1 to 9 mmHg; 3001 standard requires <3 mmHg).' That is the 2.5 mmHg Watch threshold ASTRA shows. Page 4 also records that headaches appear at 2.8-4.5 mmHg.

sources.title: MSL/RAD measured dose rate in transit and on the Martian surface
sources.note: Transit 1.84 mSv/day: Zeitlin et al., 'Measurements of Energetic Particle Radiation in Transit to Mars on the Mars Science Laboratory', Science 340(6136):1080-1084, 2013, doi 10.1126/science.1235989. Surface 0.64 mSv/day: Hassler et al., 'Mars' Surface Radiation Environment Measured with the Mars Science Laboratory's Curiosity Rover', Science 343(6176), 2014, doi 10.1126/science.1244797. These are the dose rates ASTRA shows for the transit and Mars surface environments.

sources.title: Official resource: 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight and Risks of Human Spaceflight
sources.note: Two of the five resources listed on the challenge's Resources tab on 13 Nov 2026: https://www.nasa.gov/hrp/hazards/ and https://www.nasa.gov/hrp/risks/. Neither is machine-readable, so the role is evidence. HOW IT WAS OBTAINED: each page and each of the five hazard pages it links to was read on 13 Nov 2026 and transcribed by hand into official/hrp.json: the five hazards with their page, video and the facts the pages state, and all 17 risks in the page's three categories with their own nasa.gov/reference URL. No number was added that the pages do not state. ASTRA'S PART: every risk carries an 'astra' block naming the metrics, body systems and screens that address it, and a coverage level (monitored / supported / partial). The engine test checks that every metric and body system named there exists. Gaps are named, not hidden: decompression sickness and landing loads are 'partial'. The existing HRP Roadmap citations are kept as the deeper reference (roadmap_source on each risk).

sources.title: Official resource: Ongoing HRP Research in Space
sources.note: Third resource on the challenge's Resources tab. HOW IT WAS OBTAINED: the page and the 13 ongoing studies it lists (3 for Artemis II, 10 in low Earth orbit) were read on 13 Nov 2026 and transcribed by hand into official/hrp_research.json, each with its nasa.gov/reference URL and the page's own one-line summary. The pages give no results or numbers, so none are recorded. ASTRA'S PART: each study names the HRP risks it addresses (keys of official/hrp.json) and the ASTRA measurement that is its on-board counterpart, e.g. ARCHeR (sleep, activity, well-being) and Standard Measures (sleep, cognition, strength, balance, blood). Past investigations on the page were left out because they are not ongoing.

sources.title: Official resource: CSA, Monitoring Radiation for Astronaut Health and Why Do We Conduct Science Experiments in Space?
sources.license: Government of Canada; cited and linked, not re-hosted (https://www.asc-csa.gc.ca/eng/terms.asp)
sources.note: The two Canadian Space Agency resources on the challenge's Resources tab. HOW IT WAS OBTAINED: both articles and the CSA pages they link for the instruments (MOSFET, EVARM, Radi-N2) and the infographic 'How does space affect the human body?' were read on 13 Nov 2026 and transcribed into official/csa.json, each fact with the URL it came from. KEY NUMBERS (as the CSA states them): neutrons are about 30% of ISS radiation; ISS crews receive about 150 microsieverts of neutron dose a day; spacewalk doses to skin, eyes and blood-forming organs measured about 6, 13 and 25 times nuclear-worker limits (EVARM, 2002-03); astronauts can lose up to 1.5% of bone mass a month against about 1% a year for adults over 50. These are shown as context and are NOT fed into ASTRA's dose model: the EDA station dose ASTRA uses already includes whatever its instrument sees, and adding a neutron share on top would double count. The space-agency disclaimer on the challenge page applies: NASA does not endorse non-US Government entities.
